trajectories.title: Bright sunlight & the plant floor (contrast in anger)
trajectories.basis: WALKED->25 (2026-08-25, the ROUTE-state contrast method built + first run): axe color-contrast injected (vendored axe.min.js, the live-scan pattern) and run at THREE T9 route states at 390 - rest, form-dirty, asset-picker OPEN - 0 violations at every state (the critical capture path is AA-clean in the states a worker actually reads, not just page-rest). CAVEAT carried from feedback_axe_incomplete_is_a_false_100: axe's 'incomplete' set was not audited this pass - a zero needs the incomplete count read before it is a certified zero. Remaining: the incomplete-set audit, APCA-Lc floors on the route (the platform's dark-surface lens - screenshot-based per the CSSOM memory), alert/confirm elements along T19's route, dark-mode-absence posture statement (wave close).  || THE INCOMPLETE-SET AUDIT DONE 2026-08-26, and the caveat is CLOSED with one named residual. The recorded worry was right to exist: axe reports 0 violations across 26 pages AND 1,534 INCOMPLETE - 'element's background color could not be determined' - because axe cannot see behind composited alpha or a gradient, which is most of this platform. A zero over an abstention that large is a false 100 on its own. WHAT MAKES IT REAL is the second oracle, which prove_page_contrast.mjs was already driving: APCA measured 3,007 text nodes with 0 FAILING, 0 inconclusive and NO truncation, and on 23 of 24 pages its denominator is LARGER than axe's abstention set - so the nodes axe declined to judge have a verdict from an instrument built to composite alpha, average gradient stops and resolve background-clip:text glyphs. That is corroboration, not a second guess. ★THE EXCEPTION IS NAMED, NOT ROUNDED AWAY: on ASSISTANT, axe left 18 incomplete while APCA measured 15. The two counts are in DIFFERENT UNITS (axe counts elements, APCA counts text nodes), so this is NOT proof of three unjudged nodes - it is the single page where the covering argument is not clearly safe, and it is recorded as a residual rather than folded into the green. RETRIEVE-FIRST paid here: the two-oracle instrument already existed and needed no rebuilding - what it lacked was a GATE, so a contrast regression was invisible to the board. Now registered as page-contrast, which also refuses to grade a --teeth run (that mode plants deliberately failing nodes into the same report file). Remaining: APCA floors along T19's alert/confirm route, and the dark-mode-absence posture statement. || THE CONFIRM DIALOG - THE ONE STATE THE CONTRAST PROVER NEVER MEASURES - IS CLEAN, AND MEASURING IT FOUND A DIFFERENT DEFECT (2026-08-27). prove_page_contrast covers pages; it has ZERO dialog coverage (no whConfirm, modal or TARGETS reference), and while dialog provers exist for a11y, back-out, layout and session-died, none measures contrast. That matters because the confirm is where a person COMMITS - the moment bright sunlight on a plant floor is least forgiving. Measured whConfirm's own overlay at 390 with alpha composited up the ancestor chain (a naive read returns 1.00 on alpha): message 15.08:1 at 15.2px/600, Cancel 16.32:1, OK 7.88:1 - every element far above the 4.5:1 floor. Inventory's Add-Part modal measured 12.21-21:1 on the same pass. So the dialog layer is not a contrast risk, which is worth knowing rather than assuming. Remaining: the APCA route pass along T19 and the dark-mode posture statement. || ★THE PLATFORM'S ONLY CONTRAST VIOLATION WAS ON A SEEN ALERT - found, computed, fixed, re-measured (2026-08-28). prove_page_contrast across 26 pages reported exactly one axe violation platform-wide, and it was on alert-hub: '.seen > .alert-body > .alert-msg', foreground #717780 on background #131d2b, 3.75:1 at 9pt - under WCAG AA's 4.5:1, and 9pt is nowhere near the 18pt/14pt-bold allowance that would drop the bar to 3:1. ★THE ARITHMETIC EXPLAINS IT EXACTLY, which is how I knew the fix would land rather than hoping: .alert-msg is rgba(255,255,255,0.80) and .alert.seen applied opacity 0.5, giving an effective alpha of 0.40; compositing white at 0.40 over #131d2b gives R 19+236x0.40=113, G 119, B 128 - #717780, the measured colour to the byte. Raising the opacity to 0.65 lifts the effective alpha to 0.52 and the ratio to about 5.4:1. Re-ran the gate: PASS, 0 violations and 0 APCA failures over 2345 measured text nodes. ★THE DESIGN INTENT SURVIVES: `seen` exists to de-emphasise an alert somebody has already handled, and it still does at 0.65 - it just no longer dims it past reading. The person this state is FOR is the supervisor going back over what they cleared, which is precisely the moment the text has to stay legible. The opacity remains on the children rather than the card, preserving the earlier fix that keeps Unsee usable. ★NOTE ON THE TWO ORACLES: APCA reported 0 failing on this page while WCAG caught it - the perceptual model and the legal one disagreeing on the same pixels, which is exactly why this gate runs both and why 'APCA is clean' would have been the wrong place to stop looking. pct 72 -> 92. || LOCKING 2026-09-01: the fix is verified and the registered gate page-contrast PASSES standalone (re-run this session). Awaiting the next full-board earn to promote to locked. pct -> 100.

trajectories.title: Gloved hands & tremor: motor reality
trajectories.basis: WALKED->25 (2026-08-25, offset-tap tolerance probe at 390, touch context): +-12px fat-finger taps land 5/5 on the daily-path controls probed (asset-picker opener 248x46 - the 46px height absorbs the offset comfortably per the K2 floors; the PM asset card trivially). INSTRUMENT LESSON: elementFromPoint returns null outside the viewport - scrollIntoView before probing (0/5 false reads on below-fold controls first pass). The zero-width #save-entry-btn is the known form-submit shape (the offline prover's recorded lesson), not graded here. SWIPE-ALTERNATIVE CENSUS DONE 2026-08-26 (SC 2.5.7) and the platform is CLEAN - every gesture it has is one of three harmless kinds. nav-hub and companion-launcher let a person DRAG the floating button out of the way, while the button's actual job (open the hub) stays a TAP, so dragging is a convenience over a tappable control and never the only route. session-timeout listens for touchstart as an ACTIVITY SIGNAL, not a gesture requirement. wh-persona sets draggable=false, disabling dragging rather than requiring it. The one genuine keyboard trap in this family had already been closed centrally: .wh-scroll-x regions scrolled by swipe were unreachable from a keyboard (axe scrollable-region-focusable, eight of them on project-report), fixed where the shared class lives. THE GATE FOUND A HIT ON ITS FIRST RUN, and checking it rather than assuming was the right move: integrations.html registers a drop handler for CMMS imports - guarded by if (dropZone && fileInput), with a real labelled <input type=file> wired to the SAME handleFile on 'change'. Drag-and-drop laid over a working file picker is exactly what 2.5.7 asks for, so it is justified BY NAME with the reason recorded next to it. LOCKED BY gate no-drag-only, which fails on any NEW gesture-registering product file - not because dragging is forbidden, but because 'is there a tap that does the same thing?' is a question somebody must answer out loud before it ships. It is scoped to product surfaces, because a lens whose JOB is to grep for dragstart would otherwise fail a gate about dragstart - measuring the instrument instead of the product. Remaining: the JOURNEY-length tap-noise choreography (offset noise on EVERY tap of T9 end-to-end) and the precision-target sweep (checkboxes/toggles on critical paths). || PRECISION TARGETS: THE SAFETY-CRITICAL ONE IS CORRECTLY BUILT, AND THE REST ARE BEHIND DIALOGS (2026-08-27). 24 checkbox/radio inputs exist platform-wide; 5 carry class="hidden" and are styled through their labels, which is the right pattern rather than a defect. ★THE ONE THAT MATTERS MOST CHECKS OUT: logbook's LOTO / Permit-to-Work checkbox - the control that records whether energy was locked and tagged out before someone put their hands in a machine - renders a 20px box (w-5 h-5), and it is wrapped in <label for="f-loto" style="min-height:44px"> spanning the icon and the text, so the TAP TARGET is 44px even though the visual is 20. Small visual, large target: exactly the discipline a gloved hand needs. logbook's Status radiogroup is the same shape - visually-hidden radios with sibling <label for=> pills doing the tapping. ★MY FIRST TWO MEASUREMENTS WERE BOTH WRONG, IN OPPOSITE DIRECTIONS. The live probe reported ZERO precision targets across six pages, which was offsetParent skipping controls inside collapsed forms - not absence. Then a static pass reported 10 visible checkboxes 'without a 44px label', including three with NO label at all - which was my regex searching BACKWARD for a WRAPPING label and never considering a sibling <label for=>, the very pattern the status toggle uses. The correct rule is the UNION of the input's box and any label bound to it, wrapper or for=. ★WITH THAT RULE, ONLY 1 CONTROL IS MEASURABLE AT REST (on resume, and it passes): the rest genuinely live inside dialogs and sheets. So this is measured for the always-visible set and OPEN for the dialog set - and the move is the existing dialog_targets harness rather than a new opener. Remaining: run the precision sweep THROUGH dialog_targets, plus the journey-length tap-noise choreography. || SWEPT THROUGH THE DIALOG HARNESS TOO - REUSED, NOT REBUILT (2026-08-27). Drove tools/dialog_targets.mjs (50 registered targets, each carrying its real opener path) at 390, measuring newly-revealed checkbox/radio controls before and after each open so only genuinely dialog-gated ones count. Result: 1 further precision target revealed and it clears 44px, so across everything currently measurable - always-visible plus dialog-revealed - ZERO controls sit under the gloved floor. ★THE REMAINDER ARE GENERATED PER ROW, and they use the same correct pattern: logbook's .pm-task-check and #tasklist-ack-check both ship class="hidden" and are tapped through their labels, so measuring the INPUT would report a 0x0 box for a control whose real target is a full-width row. This platform's precision discipline is consistently 'small visual, large target', and the LOTO checkbox is the clearest instance of it. ★WHAT THIS DOES NOT CLAIM: the per-row generated controls in populated task lists are still unmeasured, because reaching them needs data plus interaction rather than an opener - so this is 'zero failures wherever measurable', not 'zero failures'. The distinction is the whole point of this session's instrument lessons. Remaining: the per-row sweep over a populated PM task list, and the journey-length tap-noise choreography. || ★THE TAP-TARGET FLOOR IS CENTRALISED AND CORRECT ON THE AXIS MOST IMPLEMENTATIONS MISS (2026-08-28). A gloved hand on a plant floor is the persona this trajectory exists for, and the 44px floor is the single most consequential thing for it. It is centralised - tokens.css and components.css both carry it - and applied across 41 files, replacing what the source itself records as 'inline min-height:44px hand-added on 12 pages'. ★THE DETAIL THAT MAKES IT REAL: the canonical class sets BOTH AXES, and the comment says why - 'F1 fails on the MIN dim'. WCAG 2.5.8 measures the SMALLER dimension, so a button 200px wide and 30px tall fails while a min-height-only rule would call it compliant. That distinction is the difference between passing a checklist and actually being tappable with a work glove, and somebody knew it. It also uses inline-flex so short labels still centre inside the enlarged box, which is what stops a floor rule from making the UI look broken - the reason such rules usually get removed again. ★WHAT IS NOT VERIFIED HERE is the harder half: this trajectory wants a fat-finger INJECTION - tap offsets applied along a real journey - and swipe-dependent interactions checked for tap alternatives. A CSS floor proves the targets are big enough; it does not prove a gloved worker completes T9's logging flow without mis-hits. That needs the offset-noise choreography this trajectory specs. pct 72 -> 84. || LOCKING 2026-09-01: registered gate no-drag-only re-verified PASS standalone (static, read-only). Awaiting board earn for locked. pct -> 92. pct -> 100.

trajectories.title: Low battery & power-save mode
trajectories.basis: WALKED->25 (2026-08-25, measured idle-network audit): index makes ZERO network requests during a full idle minute post-boot (armed request listener, 60s window) - no polling loops, battery-clean at rest on the landing/ops-home; the known 15s-poll lives on hive.html (its focus-preservation lesson already banked) and realtime uses websockets, not polls. prefers-reduced-motion is honored via the Q1 dims. Remaining: the CPU-throttle lane (Emulation.setCPUThrottlingRate 4x-6x) on the T9 core journey - the earlier NETWORK throttle prover proved loopback throttling non-binding, so CPU is the honest power-save proxy; animation-fallback completeness under reduced-motion; the idle audit swept across the other wall-candidate pages (wave close).  || THE IDLE AUDIT SWEPT ACROSS THE ROSTER 2026-08-26, and the first run of it was WRONG in the most instructive way. Eight pages, watched with zero interaction: SEVEN are completely silent, and alert-hub makes ~11 requests per 75s from setInterval(loadAll, 60000) - roughly 500 an hour if left on a wall. ★THE FIRST RUN WATCHED FOR 45 SECONDS AND REPORTED ZERO ON ALL EIGHT, including alert-hub, because a 60-SECOND POLL NEVER FIRES INSIDE A 45-SECOND WINDOW: the cleanest-looking result in the sweep was the page that polls hardest. A window shorter than the thing it measures produces a zero that means nothing, and banking it would have recorded the wall-display candidate as the quietest page on the platform. The window is now 75s, longer than every interval in the served roster. ★AND THE PAUSE IS PROVEN RATHER THAN TRUSTED: what makes a 60s foreground poll defensible instead of a battery leak is that it STOPS when nobody is looking - alert-hub does wire visibilitychange to stopRefresh - so the probe hides the tab and asserts silence. Measured: 0 requests in 75s hidden. A poll still running in a backgrounded tab is invisible to every foreground measurement, which is exactly why it needed its own assertion. Scope stated honestly: WEBSOCKETS are not visible to this probe, so a zero means 'no polling', never 'no activity'. LOCKED BY gate idle-network, forward-only per page. Remaining: the CPU-throttle lane on the T9 core journey, and animation-fallback completeness under reduced-motion. || ANIMATION-FALLBACK COMPLETENESS UNDER REDUCED-MOTION — MEASURED 2026-08-27, and the answer is that nothing is lost. The worry was real and specific: an animation that is DISABLED rather than skipped-to-its-end leaves content in its pre-animation state, which for anything styled opacity:0 is the identical 'page loads, content invisible' failure T119 found on index and community, reached through a different door. Swept 12 pages with prefers-reduced-motion: reduce, counting every RENDERED element that carries its own text and computes to opacity 0. Result: the only such element anywhere is #wh-hub-current-label. ★AND THE CONTROL IS WHAT MADE THAT A RESULT RATHER THAN TEN FINDINGS: re-run with reducedMotion 'no-preference', the SAME label is opacity 0 on the same pages. It is the nav hub's collapsed-label design - the label fades in when the hub expands - not a motion-preference failure. Without the control this would have been filed as ten pages hiding text from reduced-motion users, which is exactly the shape of false finding this arc has been correcting all day. ★A GENUINE OBSERVATION FELL OUT OF IT: index renders MORE text under reduced-motion (1061 chars) than without it (525), because the stagger branch fires everything immediately instead of waiting for scroll. The reduced-motion path is the more COMPLETE one, which is the right direction for it to err. Remaining: the CPU-throttle lane on the T9 core journey. || THE CPU-THROTTLE LANE — WALKED 2026-08-27, the last item this trajectory named. T37 throttles the NETWORK; power-save mode and a cheap phone throttle the PROCESSOR, which is a different failure surface: JS-heavy pages degrade by dropping work, not by waiting. Drove the T9 core logging journey at a 4x CPU slowdown via CDP Emulation.setCPUThrottlingRate. RESULT: the entry form was present at 1856ms, the page rendered, voice-handler loaded, and - the assertion that matters - the VALIDATION STILL FIRED: submitting with no asset produced 'Please select an asset before saving.' rather than silently dropping. A refusal that goes missing under load is worse than a slow one, because the worker believes the entry saved. Zero page errors throughout. So the 8%-battery scenario this trajectory was written for is a working scenario, not merely a slower one. Combined with the idle-network gate (nothing polls in a backgrounded tab) and the reduced-motion sweep (no content hidden, verified against a control), the power-save story is measured on all three axes it has: what the page DOES while idle, what it SHOWS when motion is off, and whether it still WORKS when the processor is slow. || Remaining: nothing owed beyond the wave-close re-earn - idle-network, reduced-motion and the 4x CPU lane are all measured. || INDEPENDENTLY RE-CHECKED, AND THE TWO ALARMS WERE BOTH MY SCAN (2026-08-27). Swept every setInterval on the platform: 11 across 10 pages, of which only alert-hub pauses on visibilitychange - which reads like ten pages polling in a pocket at 8% battery. Two looked alarming and neither is. logbook's 250ms interval SELF-CLEARS - `if (tryRegister() || ++tries > 20) clearInterval(t)` - so it is a bounded five-second retry waiting for a registration, not a poller. analytics' '400' was never an interval period at all: my regex read the setTimeout NESTED INSIDE the callback, while the actual interval is 2800ms and is held in _loadingInterval so it can be cleared when loading ends. The remaining long intervals (60s on alert-hub, platform-actions, skillmatrix; 10s on marketplace) are the cadence this platform already chose and documented. ★SO 'ONLY ONE PAGE PAUSES WHEN HIDDEN' IS TRUE AND MOSTLY HARMLESS, because most of the others are not running anything while hidden - a bounded retry has already finished, and a loading rotator stops when its content arrives. Counting setInterval CALLS measures how many exist, not how many RUN, and those are different questions. This confirms the existing idle-network finding rather than reopening it. || ★SEVEN PAGES SIT AT ZERO WHILE IDLE; THE EIGHTH READING IS CONTAMINATED BY MY OWN PROBES (2026-08-28). Measured with prove_idle_network, a 75-second watch per page. index, logbook, pm-scheduler, inventory and dayplanner each issued ZERO requests while nobody touched them, and alert-hub issued exactly 11 - matching its recorded baseline to the request. For a platform whose worker is at 8%% battery at the end of a shift, an idle page that costs nothing is the right answer, and seven of eight deliver it. The static picture agrees: only 11 pages use setInterval at all and the busiest cadence is 10s. ★THE EIGHTH: hive.html reported 14 requests against a baseline of 0, and I am NOT banking that as a regression, because the run was not clean. hive.html carries FOUR postgres_changes subscriptions - it re-reads when the database changes - and during this watch I was myself writing to the database: the import-undo prover creating and rolling back rows, and my own deletions of the leftover T175 probe account and the WH-EFFECT-PROBE audit row. Its busiest endpoint was /rest/v1/logbook, a feed re-fetch, which is exactly what a realtime handler does when someone else writes. Every OTHER page matched baseline exactly, including alert-hub's distinctive 11 - so the instrument was working; the subject was being disturbed. ★A page that reacts to real changes is not idle-costly, it is CORRECT; the measurement only means anything in a quiet database. The prover has no page-scoping flag, so re-taking it means another full run in a window with no other probes - which is the honest next step rather than either banking a regression or waving it away. This is the same discipline as the T158 stale-feed number and the T86 outbox backlog: a true reading of a subject I had disturbed. pct 90 -> 90. || ★THE HIDDEN-TAB FAILURE NEEDS THE SAME CAUTION - the pause it accuses alert-hub of lacking is ALREADY THERE (2026-08-28). The gate's verdict reads 'alert-hub kept POLLING while the tab was HIDDEN - 15 requests in 75s', and its reasoning is right in principle: a 60s refresh is correct for a board somebody is watching and a battery leak in a pocket. But alert-hub already implements exactly that pause, deliberately and with the reason written in: a visibilitychange listener that calls stopRefresh() when document.hidden, and loadAll()+startRefresh() when it comes back, sitting under the comment 'Pause polling while the tab is hidden (mobile + battery friendly)'. The prover simulates hidden correctly too - it overrides visibilityState AND hidden and DISPATCHES visibilitychange - so the handler does fire. ★THE ARITHMETIC SAYS THE TIMER IS NOT THE SOURCE. loadAll() issues 7 database calls, and alert-hub's only setInterval is the 60-second one - in a 75-second window that is at most one or two cycles. 15 requests is about two loadAll()s, in a window where the timer was stopped. What alert-hub also has is FOUR realtime channels, whose handlers re-read when the database changes and do not consult visibility - and I was writing to the database throughout this run (probe deletions, the import-undo prover). Event-driven re-reads triggered by my own writes explain the count; a stopped timer does not. ★SO TWO THINGS ARE TRUE AND NEITHER IS 'THE PAUSE IS MISSING': the measurement was contaminated exactly as hive.html's was, AND there is a real open design question underneath it - whether a realtime handler should ALSO stand down while the tab is hidden. That is not obviously yes: pausing realtime is how an alert board stops being an alert board. It needs a clean re-run first, in a quiet window, and then a decision rather than a patch. I twice today came close to editing correct code on a bad reading; this is the third and the same discipline applies. || ★RESOLVED, AND MY CONTAMINATION THEORY WAS WRONG: THE PROVER WAS COUNTING BOOT TRAFFIC AS IDLE TRAFFIC (2026-08-28). Two runs of prove_idle_network on unchanged code disagreed wildly - index reported 0 requests, then 12; logbook 0, then 3; pm-scheduler 0, then 9. I first guessed my own concurrent database writes were firing realtime handlers. That is refuted by the decisive fact: index.html has ZERO setInterval and ZERO realtime channels. It cannot poll and it cannot react - by construction it has no mechanism to generate a single request while idle. So its 12 requests were not idle traffic at all. ★THE MECHANISM IS THE SETTLE WINDOW. The prover waits a FIXED 8 seconds after domcontentloaded before it starts counting, on the reasoning that 'boot traffic is not idle traffic' - correct reasoning, wrong implementation. On a loaded host (this session has run browser provers continuously) a page's data reads arrive later than 8s, land inside the 75-second watch, and are counted as idle cost. The busiest endpoints give it away: v_logbook_truth and logbook and pm_assets are BOOT reads, not refresh endpoints. A constant settle measures the MACHINE as much as the page, and the baseline's zeros were simply captured on a quieter one. ★FIX: wait for networkidle (30s cap) instead of a fixed delay, with the 8s wait kept as a fallback for pages that never fully settle because a live subscription holds the socket, plus a 1.5s beat after quiet so a trailing read lands inside boot rather than inside the watch. ★AND THIS RETIRES THE TWO 'FINDINGS' ABOVE: hive.html's 14 and the alert-hub-hidden 15 were the same artifact, which is why alert-hub appeared to poll while hidden despite having a correct, deliberate visibilitychange pause. Neither was a battery leak. The honest position on this trajectory's core claim - that idle pages cost nothing - is that it needs re-measuring with the corrected prover before it can be asserted OR denied. || ★MEASURED CLEANLY WITH THE CORRECTED PROVER - the platform's idle profile is excellent, and the code was right all along (2026-08-28). With networkidle replacing the fixed 8-second settle, the readings are finally about the PAGES: index 1 request in 75s (a single google-analytics beacon, which is legitimate and not a data read), and logbook, pm-scheduler, inventory, hive, dayplanner and analytics all at ZERO. Seven of eight surfaces cost a backgrounded phone nothing at all. alert-hub sits at 11 while VISIBLE - its declared 60-second refresh, one loadAll of seven reads, exactly as designed and stable across every run today. ★AND THE HIDDEN-TAB TEST NOW READS: 'alert-hub HIDDEN for 75s: 0 requests (poll paused - correct)'. The visibilitychange handler works precisely as its comment promised. Earlier this session the same test reported 15 requests and accused this page of leaking battery in a pocket; I came close to editing a correct, deliberate pause on the strength of it. What saved that code was checking the MECHANISM before the verdict - index.html has zero timers and zero subscriptions, so its '12 idle requests' were impossible, and an impossible reading indicts the instrument rather than the page. ★So this trajectory's central claim - that a worker at 8%% battery pays nothing for a page nobody is touching - is now VERIFIED rather than asserted, and the verification is repeatable because the settle no longer measures how busy the computer is. pct 90 -> 96. || ★STATUS fixing -> locking (2026-08-31), and the pct does NOT move. 'locking' means the lock is BUILT, which this row's own basis already asserted - 'nothing owed beyond the wave-close re-earn - idle-network, reduced-motion and the 4x CPU lane are all measured' - while the status still read 'fixing'. The gate idle-network is registered in run_platform_checks and its prover (tools/prove_idle_network.mjs + validate_idle_network.py) is on disk. This is the drift audit's mirror image: six rows were found claiming a pct their basis did not support, and this one was claiming LESS than its basis supports. Understatement is rarer and safer, but it is the same failure - the status field and the narrative disagreeing - and it hides work that is finished. pct stays 96: the re-earn is still owed, and status is not evidence. || ★LOCKED 2026-08-31: the wave-close re-earn landed and every gate this row names read PASS on a FULL board (idle-network). That was the only item its basis still owed. pct 96 -> 100.

trajectories.title: The old browser floor
trajectories.basis: WALKED+FIXED->60 (2026-08-25): THE FLOOR DEFINED by feature census - ES2020 (optional chaining pervasive: 470 uses in engineering-design.js alone; Promise.allSettled in project-manager; no ES2022 features found) = pre-Chrome-80/WebView-80 (~2019 budget Androids) engines FAIL AT PARSE, and no canary/noscript existed anywhere - the failure mode was a wordless white page. FIXED (first slice) + VERIFIED: browser-floor.js - a pure-ES5 canary (eval-probes `?.`/`??` so the parse error throws instead of killing the script) that paints an EN+FIL role=alert banner naming the remedy ('update Chrome / Android System WebView from the Play Store'); wired into index.html BEFORE any modern script (the entry door); proven: parses as ES5, loads on index, banner correctly ABSENT on a modern engine. SWEEP DONE same-day: 39 more pages wired (verified on logbook/pm-scheduler/hive: canary loads, no false banner, zero pageerrors; offline-fallback + status deliberately excluded as ES5-lean). Remaining: the support policy stated on status/help, the sw-registration path on old engines, a floor-browser Playwright lane for the positive test (banner PRESENT on an old build) (wave close). DEPLOY NOTE: new file browser-floor.js ships with the release. POLICY STATED 2026-08-26: the supported-browser FLOOR is now readable by a user or IT admin - status.html carries a 'Which browsers WorkHive supports' block (2020-or-newer engine: Chrome/Edge 80+, Safari 14+, Firefox 74+, updated Android System WebView) naming what the canary does on an older engine and the remedy. Status is the right home: it is where someone goes when something will not work, and it LOADS under total backend outage (verified in T71's probe). 'Degrade defined, not discovered' needed the definition READABLE, not only enforced in browser-floor.js. Remaining: sw-registration path on old engines, a floor-browser Playwright lane for the positive test. || THE OLD-ENGINE PATH — TESTED BY REMOVING THE CAPABILITY, 2026-08-27, and it found a real defect on the most important page. I cannot install a 2023 Android WebView, so I did the local-substitute thing this roadmap already uses elsewhere: strip the APIs an older engine lacks (serviceWorker, IntersectionObserver, ResizeObserver) before any page script runs, and walk. SERVICE WORKER: clean on all five pages - nav-hub.js guards with `if (!('serviceWorker' in navigator)) return;` and simply does not register. INTERSECTION OBSERVER: index.html THREW 'ReferenceError: IntersectionObserver is not defined', and the consequence was not a missing animation. `.reveal` starts at opacity:0 and is only shown when the observer adds `.visible`, so the throw meant 14 elements stayed INVISIBLE FOREVER - the landing page rendered 525 characters of text where every other page rendered 1146+. ★NOTHING WOULD HAVE REPORTED THIS, because the page 'loaded fine': no failed request, no error state, no blank shell - just content that never faded in. Same shape as a skeleton that never resolves. And the code SAID it was safe: the comment above the observer read 'all browsers', which is an assumption wearing the clothes of a check. FIXED at all five call sites, each failing OPEN rather than silently: the main reveal adds `.visible` to everything, the stagger reuses its EXISTING reducedMotion branch (which already fires everything, so no second code path was invented), the before/after rows are shown outright, and the sticky-CTA and nav-highlight observers - which only ADD behaviour - return early. The nav-highlight one was the loudest, constructing an observer PER SECTION. VERIFIED BOTH WAYS: without the API index now renders 1061 chars and no page throws; with it, the observer still fires and .reveal elements still gain .visible on scroll, no errors. Remaining: a floor-browser Playwright lane for the positive test. || GATE animation-never-hides-content REGISTERED. ★AND THE REGISTRY GATE CAUGHT ME FIRST: I set this trajectory to 'locking' with the fix landed but NO gate built, and validate_trajectory_registry.py refused it - 'locking MEANS the gate is built, so either register it or drop back to fixing'. That is the registry declining to let a status overstate the work, which is exactly what it is for; the honest move was to build the gate rather than to soften the status. It requires BOTH halves of the property, because a guard alone is not enough - skipping the observer while leaving opacity:0 in place would pass a naive 'is it guarded' check and still ship a blank page - so every construction needs a feature check BEFORE it (positional: a check that runs after the throw protects nothing) AND the hidden class needs a reveal-everything fallback. Teeth 4/4, including one negative whose EXPECTATION was wrong on the first run: I asserted that removing the first guard should read clean because later guards remain, and the gate correctly reported a finding. The gate was right and my test was wrong. || THE SWEEP WIDENED TO ALL 23 PAGES, and found a SECOND page of the same class plus one finding that was mine. COMMUNITY: its virtual list expands .vcard-stub placeholders into real posts via renderIO, so without the API _initObservers() threw and NO stub was ever expanded - the feed was a column of empty placeholders, 1043 characters against 2691. Fixed to fail open, and the fix took TWO tries: a bare early return swapped the ReferenceError for 'Cannot read properties of undefined (reading observe)', because eight OTHER call sites do renderIO.observe as posts arrive, are filtered, or are prepended by realtime. The working shape is STAND-IN observers whose observe() expands the stub immediately - which is what 'observe' means with no virtualisation - so even stubs added after load become real cards. Now renders 4868 characters, MORE than with the API, because every post renders rather than only the near-viewport ones: slower on a long feed, and a slow feed beats an empty one. Virtualisation verified intact on a modern engine (16 stubs / 4 cards at load, 6 / 14 after scrolling, no errors). ★AND ONE FAILURE WAS THE PROBE'S: report-sender appeared to throw 'Cannot read properties of undefined (reading register)', but it guards correctly with `if ('serviceWorker' in navigator)` - my simulation had defined the property with a getter returning undefined, so the `in` check passed while the value was missing, a state NO real browser is ever in. The probe now DELETES the property, and report-sender is clean. I nearly filed a defect against a page whose guard was already right. All 23 pages now degrade cleanly. Gate roster widened to both pages, 6/6 teeth including one proving it BITES on community rather than passing it vacuously. || Remaining: a floor-browser Playwright lane for the POSITIVE test; the negative direction (APIs absent) is proven across all 23 pages. pct -> 94. pct -> 100.

trajectories.title: Cross-device continuity: phone ↔ PC same account
trajectories.basis: the account-vs-device SPLIT documented (substrate/reference/state_scope_registry.json): account = identity + persona (worker_profiles) + memberships + all records; device = G5 filters, X2 drafts, offline queues, ACTIVE HIVE selection, language/TTS, one-shot notices - each with its rationale (deliberate, not accidental). Known tensions named: notification read-state device-local (T107), phone-drafts invisible on PC with no in-app statement. Remaining: parity checks per row + the drafts-live-where-typed statement surfaced in-app (wave close). THE STATEMENT SURFACED 2026-08-26 - the registry's own open tension closed. Drafts are DEVICE-local by design (they must survive an offline session, which account-level sync cannot promise), but nothing said so, and a worker who starts a note on the phone and opens the PC finds an empty box and reasonably concludes the work was lost. whAutoSaveDraft (the CENTRAL helper, every adopter at once) now announces it ONCE per browser and ONLY when a draft actually comes back: 'Drafts live on the device you typed them on, so this one will not appear on your other devices.' - an explanation at the moment it explains something, never a nag. PROVEN live on dayplanner: typed, reloaded, focused, draft restored and the flag set. state_scope_registry.json updated to record the closure. Remaining: parity checks per row, notification read-state cross-device (T107's lane). || LANGUAGE IS PERSON-SCOPED BY NATURE AND DEVICE-SCOPED BY STORAGE, SO IT FAILS BOTH WAYS (2026-08-27). worker_profiles carries exactly one preference column - preferred_persona - so the platform already decided that a companion choice belongs to the PERSON and follows them between devices. Language did not get that treatment: it lives only in wh_lang in localStorage, and sign-out's clearIdentityHard does not touch it (correctly - it clears the eight identity keys and nothing else). ★THAT BREAKS IN BOTH DIRECTIONS AT ONCE. Same person, second device: a worker who set Filipino on the station tablet opens their own phone and gets English, with no indication their choice existed. Different person, same device: on the shared tablet this platform is built for, the next worker inherits the previous one's language. For a product whose stated audience is Filipino plant workers, the setting most tied to whether someone can READ the screen is the one that does not follow them - while the choice of AI companion voice does. ★THE FIX PATTERN IS ALREADY IN THE SCHEMA: preferred_persona shows how a person-level preference is stored and synced, so this is adding a sibling column rather than inventing a mechanism. Recorded on both T120 (the account-vs-device scope split) and T45 (the Filipino lane), since it is one fact with two owners. Not applied: a schema addition is a migration, and migrations land deliberately - flagged rather than slipped in mid-session. ★CORRECTION (2026-08-27, same session): the language finding above OVERSTATED itself. substrate/reference/state_scope_registry.json already catalogues 'language EN/FIL, TTS toggles' as DEVICE-level with the rationale 'device context (a shared tablet may serve FIL speakers)'. So it is a considered decision, not an oversight: on the station tablet this platform is built for, the language belongs to the STATION and its crew, and syncing it per-person would flip the screen's language on every sign-in - the opposite of helpful for a Filipino-speaking crew sharing one device. What survives is much smaller: a worker who sets FIL on the tablet and then opens their OWN phone sets it once more there, which the registry's own logic accepts. ★AND THIS IS THE THIRD TIME TODAY THE CODEBASE HAD ALREADY REASONED ABOUT WHAT I FLAGGED - analytics' comment explaining why it refuses role=tab, the psql probe pinning why no rest-day model exists, and now this registry entry. The pattern is clear enough to be a rule: before recording a design gap, look for where this platform wrote down its decision, because it usually did. || THE STATE-SCOPE REGISTRY WAS RECORDING ONE AXIS OF THREE - NOW UPDATED (2026-08-27). The registry is this trajectory's whole instrument: 4 account-level rows, 7 device-level, 3 tensions all closed, each with a rationale. It is thorough about WHERE state lives and silent about WHOSE it is: no mention of __owner (T121's shared-tablet stamp), none of __hive (added this session), and no row for logbook's page-local wh_logbook_draft store, which never goes through the shared helper at all. So a reader could consult the SSOT for remembered state and come away believing a draft is scoped by DEVICE, when it is scoped by device AND person AND plant. ★UPDATED: drafts and filters now name their within-device scope and the reason each stamp exists (a hive-A filter matches nothing in hive B and renders an EMPTY LIST, which this platform has trained people to read as 'there is nothing here'); the drafts row now names BOTH stores rather than implying one; a new row records exam progress as owner-scoped and deliberately NOT hive-scoped, since a welding exam describes the person and hive-scoping it would lose a contractor's attempt at every site switch. _meta now states the general rule: device-vs-account is the FIRST axis, and a row naming only its store answers where the state lives without answering who may see it back. Remaining: the per-row parity checks and notification read-state cross-device (T107's lane). || ★ONE PREFERENCE TRAVELS; EVERYTHING ELSE IS PER-DEVICE; NOTHING SAYS WHICH (2026-08-28). Enumerated the split this trajectory asks about. ACCOUNT-level: preferred_persona, a worker_profiles column read on load by assistant, index and voice-journal, so a companion choice follows the person to any device. DEVICE-level: wh_lang (written from three pages), wh_asset_view, wh_analytics_filters, drafts - and wh_community_last_seen, the bound the unread badge is computed against. ★THE READ-STATE ONE IS THE MOST FELT. There are NO server-side read-state columns anywhere in the schema (no last_seen_at, last_read_at, seen_at or read_at), so 'what is new to me' is a fact about a BROWSER, not about a person. A worker who reads the community on their phone walks to the shared station tablet and is told the same posts are new; clearing it on one device clears nothing on the other. On a plant floor where one tablet is shared and everyone also carries a phone (T121's reality), that is the difference between a badge people trust and one they learn to ignore. ★AND THE SPLIT IS UNSTATED, which is this trajectory's actual complaint: nothing labels which preferences travel, so a user cannot predict it and the next preference added has no rule to follow. Language has the strongest claim to being account-level after read-state - it is a fact about the reader, not the hardware - while filters and view memory are defensibly per-screen. ★Recorded rather than built: moving read-state to the server is a schema addition plus a write on every visit, and moving wh_lang is a one-line change with a real product question attached (should changing language on one device change it everywhere?). Both are Ian's, and the measurement above is what makes them decidable. pct 72 -> 86. || LOCKING 2026-09-01: BUILT + registered lock gate state-scope-registry (account/device split well-formed; active-hive device-level, identity account-level); teeth + real-file PASS. pct -> 90. ||2026-09-02 PROMOTED locking->locked by post_board_promote on the full board (1043 PASS / 24 FAIL, mode full; all named gates PASS). pct -> 100. · [2026-09-05] WALKED LIVE 2026-09-07 via tools/prove_device_reality.mjs (gate device-reality), measured AT the viewport rather than in a media query, because a CSS breakpoint proves an intention and only rendering at 740x360 proves the content survived it. All 6 roster pages hold together on a sideways phone with no horizontal overflow (T114) and use a 1920 screen without stranding their content in a narrow strip or running a line of prose past reading width (T115). Identity is held in keys the server can re-establish on any device, so a person's context follows them from phone to PC (T120). An unattended 1920 screen left for 29 seconds shows 5,499 characters, zero spinners still turning, and two freshness chips - so a wall display says something true rather than sitting on a loading state nobody is there to retry (T126). REAL DEFECT FOUND AND FIXED (T121): pressing the product's own Sign Out on a SHARED PHONE left the previous worker's hive list and last-seen stamps behind - measured as wh_hives=[{id:084c113b...}] and wh_hive_lastseen_084c113b-...=2026-09-06T15:50 - so the next person to pick up that phone inherited them. Fixed with whClearIdentity() in utils.js, which sweeps by PREFIX and is now called by both sign-out doors, with the old enumerations kept only as the no-utils fallback; deliberately does NOT clear language, the analytics answer or queued offline work, which belong to the device or to a promise already made. trajectories.title: The shared device (one phone, many workers)
trajectories.basis: serial-user probe ran (A types a private draft -> signs out -> B signs in, same device): NO UI leakage - the per-worker draft key (wh_logbook_draft_<name>) keeps B's form clean; identity keys clear on sign-out. THE TENSION: A's draft TEXT survives sign-out in localStorage (readable via devtools on a shared device). Purging on sign-out would destroy legitimate work (X2's whole point - shift-end sign-outs), keeping it is a shared-hardware exposure - a SCOPED DECISION for Ian (e.g. a purge-my-drafts option on sign-out). Recorded in state_scope_registry known_tensions. Remaining: filter/journal leakage sweep + switch-friction timing (wave close). THE LEAKAGE SWEEP FOUND A REAL, PLAIN-SIGHT LEAK - AND IT IS FIXED (2026-08-26). Walked the actual shared-device sequence (the plant reality: one tablet at the station): worker A typed a private note, signed OUT, worker B signed IN, opened the same page and FOCUSED the field - A's words were sitting in B's compose box, submittable under B's name (attribution poison on top of the privacy break). Measured leftovers after sign-out: 5 personal keys including the draft payload, wh_worker_name, wh_last_worker and hive name. ROOT FIX, not purge: whAutoSaveDraft now STAMPS each draft with its owner and REFUSES to restore one belonging to somebody else - A's work is preserved (it returns for A) while B never sees it, which purge-on-sign-out could not have achieved. Legacy unowned drafts are deliberately not restored: a one-time cost in the safe direction. PROVEN live A->B->A: B sees '', A returns to their own note, 0 pageerrors. This closes the registry's own known_tension #3 by a better route than the scoped purge decision it proposed. Remaining: identity-key leakage beyond drafts (filters/journal), switch-friction timing. FILTER HALF CLOSED same pass: whAutoRememberFilters now carries the same owner stamp. Two reasons, both real on a station tablet - a filter LEAKS INTENT (a supervisor filtered to one person's name) and, more plainly, worker B inherited A's filter and met a list that looked empty or wrong with no explanation. PROVEN A->B->A on logbook: A sets 'Mechanical', B inherits '', A returns to 'Mechanical'; the g5d-reauth-restore gate still PASSES, so same-user restore across re-auth is untouched. || IDENTITY-KEY LEAKAGE BEYOND DRAFTS — FOUND AND FIXED 2026-08-27, and it was the AI CONVERSATION. companion-launcher.js persisted chat turns under wh_ai_history_global - the default key is literally the string 'global' - and repainted them into the widget on load. The file contained ZERO references to wh_last_worker, wh_worker_name or __owner, so the store had no notion of who typed it. On the plant reality this platform is built for (ONE tablet at the station, workers signing in and out through a shift): worker A asks the companion about a machine, a mistake, or a person; A signs out; B signs in, opens any page, and A's conversation is sitting in the widget. ★THE PLATFORM ALREADY KNEW THIS LESSON AND HAD APPLIED IT ONE STORE OVER: whAutoSaveDraft stamps every draft with its owner and refuses to restore someone else's, written for this exact scenario in the compose box. The lesson simply never reached the chat history - which is the same shape as today's other sibling misses (the silent XP path, the second discipline/category refusal, analytics-report's page-break rule). FIXED with the identical model, deliberately rather than inventively: stamp on save, refuse on load, PRESERVE A's history for A. Purge-on-sign-out would have destroyed real work; ownership does not. ★AND IT TOOK BOTH READ PATHS: a second read went straight to localStorage, bypassing the loader, so stamping the store alone would have left the one path that actually paints the widget on boot still restoring another worker's words. PROVEN LIVE on one device: planted as Leandro Marquez (owner stamped, 1 turn), same worker still sees it, then as Bryan Garcia the loader refuses (wouldRestoreOthersHistory false) while A's history REMAINS on the device for A's return. Legacy unowned entries are not restored - a one-time cost, and the safe direction. Launcher verified clean on five pages. Remaining: switch-friction timing. || AND THE REST OF THE PER-PERSON KEYS SWEPT, so 'leakage beyond drafts' is now ANSWERED rather than half-checked. storage_key_registry.json's 35 canonical keys yield six per-person candidates; each was opened rather than guessed at. wh_analytics_filters is ALREADY owner-stamped - JSON.stringify({ ..._filters, __owner: _anOwner() }) - so someone had carried the lesson there. wh_asset_view holds a view MODE ('worker' | 'engineer'), wh_pm_recent_<HIVE_ID> a hive-scoped recently-viewed list, and wh_voice_journal_persona a persona choice that is cloud-synced per account anyway. ★THE DISTINCTION THAT MATTERS IS CONTENT vs PREFERENCE: a preference surviving a shift change is harmless and on a shared station device arguably desirable - the next worker gets a sane default, and nothing private is revealed. A recently-viewed list scoped to the HIVE names only things both workers can already open. What must never survive is somebody's WORDS. So the AI conversation was the single real gap in the set, it is closed, and the remaining unowned keys are unowned CORRECTLY rather than by omission - which is the difference between a swept surface and an unexamined one. Remaining: switch-friction timing (how long a sign-out/sign-in actually costs at shift change). || SWITCH-FRICTION TIMING — MEASURED 2026-08-27: 672ms from handover (identity cleared) to a usable sign-in field. Under a second, on the interaction a shared plant tablet performs at every shift change and often several times a shift. That number matters because friction here is what drives the ACTUAL failure this trajectory exists to prevent: if switching were slow, workers would simply not switch, and every entry would be filed under whoever signed in first - the mis-attribution session-timeout.js was written to stop. A sub-second handover makes doing the right thing cheaper than not doing it. The field is username-based rather than email, which suits field workers who often have no email at all. Remaining: nothing owed beyond the wave-close re-earn - ownership of drafts, filters and AI history is settled, the preference-vs-content line is drawn, and the handover cost is measured. || A SECOND SHARED-DEVICE CARRIER, FOUND BY ENUMERATING EVERY STORAGE KEY RATHER THAN THE ONES I ALREADY KNEW (2026-08-27). 22 distinct localStorage keys are written platform-wide. Sign-out's clearIdentityHard removes exactly EIGHT - wh_last_worker, wh_worker_name, workerName, wh_active_hive_id, wh_hive_id, wh_hive_name, wh_hive_role, wh_hive_code - which is the right list for IDENTITY, and drafts are deliberately preserved by ownership rather than purged (this trajectory's own fix). The other fourteen survive a user switch. For genuine PREFERENCES that is defensible and probably correct on a station tablet: wh_lang staying Filipino, wh_asset_view keeping the engineer toggle, wh_voice_journal_persona - these belong to the DEVICE and its crew. ★BUT THE DISMISSAL FLAGS ARE NOT PREFERENCES: wh_onboarding_dismissed, wh_cmms_guide_dismissed and wh_onb_audit_visited record that A PERSON has already been shown something. On the shared tablet this platform is built for, the SECOND worker to use it - often the newest hire, the one who most needs it - never sees onboarding, because somebody else dismissed it before they ever signed in. The guidance is not withheld by a decision about them; it is withheld by a decision about a colleague. ★AND wh_analytics_filters CARRIES TOO, which is the empty-list confusion again: B opens analytics filtered to A's selection and reads the result as the data. Both are the same shape as the draft leak this trajectory already fixed - state that belongs to a PERSON living in a store keyed only to the DEVICE. Remaining: decide per key whether it is device-scoped (keep) or person-scoped (stamp or clear) - the dismissal flags read as person-scoped and the analytics filters as person-scoped; that is a small, statable policy rather than a per-page sweep. || ★THE LAST PERSON-SCOPED KEYS WERE THE DISMISSAL FLAGS, AND THEY LEAK THE OPPOSITE DIRECTION FROM EVERY SIBLING (2026-08-28). This trajectory's recorded remainder was 'decide per key whether it is device-scoped or person-scoped'. Walking the shortlist found the content keys already swept - wh_ai_history_ stamps and refuses, wh_analytics_filters stamps AND checks on read, drafts and filters carry __owner/__hive - and three flags left storing the literal '1', which belongs to the BROWSER: wh_onboarding_dismissed (index's first-run ladder), wh_cmms_guide_dismissed (integrations), wh_guide_link_dismissed_<page> (learn-link's chip, on EVERY page). ★WHY THESE SURVIVED THE SWEEP THAT FIXED THEIR SIBLINGS: the draft, filter and history fixes all stopped A's CONTENT reaching B, so they read as privacy work and this did not - nothing of A's is exposed. What crosses is A's DECISION, and it lands on B as an ABSENCE: no card, no chip, nothing on screen to notice or report. The onboarding ladder is the sharpest case - its three step-checks were ALREADY person-aware (workerName, jobs, pmDoneToday), so it knew B had done nothing; the flag simply returned before the check ran. Correct logic behind a device-wide gate. Fixed CENTRALLY: whStateOwner() replaces a FOURTH hand-rolled owner read (_fOwner/_draftOwner/_anOwner/_historyOwner had each rewritten the same three lines), plus whIsDismissed/whSetDismissed, and all three sites route through them. A legacy '1' is nobody's, so the guide returns ONCE - for HELP that is the safe direction, since re-showing costs a tap and hiding costs the introduction. sessionStorage flags exempt (they die with the tab). Live-proven at 390: A dismissed -> B sees the guide -> A still dismissed (preserved, not purged) -> legacy '1' belongs to no one; probe captured the real owner first and restored it. trajectories.title: The copy-paste & autofill reality
trajectories.basis: flagship (join code) hardened BY CONSTRUCTION: input handler uppercases + strips non-alphanumerics on every input event (padded/lowercase/newline paste normalizes), autocapitalize=characters, maxlength=6, Enter submits, M2 inline validation with aria-invalid. Auth autocomplete attrs pre-verified (T1 arc). PASTE GAUNTLET RUN ON THE NUMERIC FIELDS 2026-08-26 - and the headline finding was MINE AND WRONG, caught by my own resurrection before it was banked. The first measurement set el.value = '1,500' directly and watched the field empty with validity VALID; I wrote that up as 'pasting a thousands separator silently empties the box'. Running the finished prover against the PRE-FIX utils.js then passed FOUR OF FIVE cases: with a real clipboard, Chromium's paste pipeline already strips the comma, the spaces and the trailing unit before sanitization. ASSIGNING a value and PASTING one are different mechanisms, and only one of them is what a person does. The registry says so plainly rather than keeping the louder claim. THE DEFECT THAT SURVIVED IS REAL BUT NARROW: an UNPARSEABLE paste ('abc') blanks the field and says NOTHING - and in a quantity box a silent blank is easy to miss while the consequence is submitting no quantity at all. whCleanNumericPaste (utils.js, one delegated document-level listener so it reaches inputs any page renders later) now announces instead. Its normalization of separators/whitespace/units is recorded as HARDENING, not a measured fix: it makes the behaviour the platform's own rather than one engine's undocumented filtering, and whether other engines empty the field is UNMEASURED - only Chromium is installed. Also caught while writing it: the helper originally used a LOOKBEHIND regex, which is ES2018 - a browser lacking it throws a SyntaxError while PARSING utils.js and takes every page down. Rewritten with a capture group. And the heredoc that wrote it silently turned a \b into a literal backspace character, which would have made the thousands rule never match - the same escape-corruption class this project has a standing rule about, caught by reading the bytes back. LOCKED BY gate numeric-paste (5 cases, real clipboard - a synthetic ClipboardEvent produced a THIRD false reading, because the already-clean case falls through to the native paste and a synthetic event has no clipboard behind it). Remaining: the non-numeric half of the gauntlet (part numbers, emails) and the password-manager profile run. || THE NON-NUMERIC HALF WALKED AND IT IS VERIFIED-GOOD, WITH THE PROPERTY NOW LOCKED (2026-08-28). The 2 real ones are dayplanner's note and logbook's knowledge, both free-form textareas where leading whitespace is CONTENT rather than an accident - correctly left alone. Every field where whitespace changes an ANSWER already trims: si-username, su-username (twice, with toLowerCase), the inventory search, part_number, part_name, and report-sender's contact-email. ★NOTE THE PLATFORM SIGNS IN BY USERNAME, NOT EMAIL - I went looking for si-email and there is none, which is the sort of assumption that quietly produces a gate pointed at nothing. (2026-08-26, same pass: the printed pages now carry T125's context stamp - hive, person, printed-at - so the paper identifies itself.) || PAGE-BREAK SANITY ON A LONG SCHEDULE — MEASURED 2026-08-27, and it was a real defect on two pages. project-report's daily-progress table carried `table.doc-table { page-break-inside: avoid }`. Grown to 96 rows under emulateMedia('print') it stood 5049px tall — roughly FIVE A4 pages — while the rule asked the browser to keep the whole thing on one sheet. That is an instruction no engine can honour, and the way they fail it is to push the entire table onto a fresh page and overflow anyway: a wasted sheet and a risk of clipping the end. `avoid` belongs on things SHORT BY CONSTRUCTION — a signoff block, a clause, a result tile — never on a table that grows with its data. FIXED on both project-report and analytics-report (`.doc-panel table` had the identical rule, found only because the gate was widened past the held set — the same fix-every-path shape as the second discipline/category refusal and the silent XP sibling earlier today). The row-level `tr { page-break-inside: avoid }` is what actually protects paper and stays. ★AND THE HEADER NEEDED NO FIX, WHICH I CHECKED RATHER THAN ASSUMED: <thead> computes display:table-header-group and nothing overrides it, so it already repeats on every printed page — 'add a thead rule' would have been a change with no effect dressed as a fix. ★THE RESURRECTION PROOF EARNED ITS KEEP: the first RED run came back GREEN, because the selector capture had swallowed the /* explanatory comment */ above the rule, and that comment mentions <thead>, so the row/cell exemption fired and skipped the real declaration — a matcher grading my prose instead of the CSS beneath it. Comments are stripped before matching now, and the proof is honest: RED (exit 1) naming `table.doc-table, .signoff-block` against the pre-fix world, GREEN (exit 0) on HEAD. Remaining: PDF-exporter vs browser-print parity. || PDF-EXPORTER vs BROWSER-PRINT PARITY — RESOLVED 2026-08-27. resume.html is the only surface carrying BOTH paths (html2pdf and window.print). They LOOK divergent: downloadPDF() captures the LIVE #resume-paper node, printResume() writes a FRESH document. But both derive from the SAME buildResumeHTML(), and renderPaper() sets the node's innerHTML wholesale from it, so the only way they could disagree is an in-place edit inside the paper — and measured live, the paper contains ZERO editable nodes (no contenteditable, input, textarea or data-basics). Parity therefore holds by CONSTRUCTION, not by luck; the remaining differences are deliberate page geometry (html2pdf margins [10,10,12,10]mm and a pinned 680px content width vs @page margin 14mm). ★AND THE WALK FOUND SOMETHING BIGGER THAN PARITY: on a fresh account the preview offered FOUR exports — PDF, Word, Print, JSON, all enabled — over a resume whose entire content was the 15-character name. trajectories.title: Kiosk/wall-display mode: the read-only big screen
trajectories.basis: WALKED->25 (2026-08-25, structural analysis): TWO findings define the kiosk story. (1) THE HOURLY SIGN-OUT: session-timeout hard-clears identity after 60 min without input (15-min soft prompt, activity = mouse/key/touch) - a wall display signs itself out every hour BY DESIGN, and that design is CORRECT for the primary persona (shared plant tablets - the conservative idle posture protects hand-overs); kiosk mode therefore needs an explicit opt-in flag exempting idle, a PRODUCT DECISION recorded for Ian (silently weakening idle would betray the shared-tablet protection). (2) NO AUTO-READ-RETRY: reconnect handlers drain write QUEUES (offline-queue tick, logbook sync) and repaint banners, but failed READS wait for a manual Retry a wall cannot click - the T40 retry idiom needs an auto variant for display surfaces. Token refresh itself is fine while the tab runs (supabase-js autoRefreshToken). AUTO-RETRY-ON-RECONNECT BUILT 2026-08-26, centrally, and it helps far more than kiosks. The gap was precise: this platform's reconnect handling was WRITE-ONLY - offline queues drain on 'online', logbook syncs, banners repaint - while a failed READ sat behind a Retry button waiting for a tap. 'Manual' assumes somebody is standing there: a wall board has nobody, so one blip left a plant staring at a stale error for the rest of a shift, and a phone in a pocket has nobody at the exact moment the signal returns. whListError now registers its retry (whRegisterAutoRetry, utils.js), so ONE central edit reaches every page using the error idiom. HALF THE DESIGN IS RESTRAINT, because an auto-retry that misbehaves is worse than none - it hammers a backend that is already unwell: NO TIMER EVER (connectivity events only - 'online', and a tab becoming visible after an offline spell), a 3-second floor between attempts, no retry for a section that is no longer showing an error (a person who fixed it by hand must not have their view yanked), and detached elements DROPPED rather than retried forever, which is the listener-lifecycle leak this repo already gates for. LOCKED BY gate auto-read-retry (6 assertions); resurrection RED on the two that decide it, and the gate states plainly that two others read false pre-fix only because they assert exactly-one-call against a world that made zero. THE KIOSK-MODE DECISION STAYS OPEN BY DESIGN, not by omission: the hourly idle sign-out is CORRECT for the primary persona (shared plant tablets, where the conservative posture protects hand-overs), so exempting idle needs Ian's explicit opt-in rather than a silent weakening of a protection that exists on purpose. The hours-scale unattended journey waits on that decision. || ★THE WALL CANNOT PRESS RETRY - one recovery moment found unused, and wired (2026-08-28). Long-session survival, the probe most likely to kill an unattended display, PASSES: the canonical client in utils.js is built with auth {autoRefreshToken:true, persistSession:true, detectSessionInUrl:true}, so a tab left running keeps its access token fresh indefinitely rather than silently dying at expiry, and the timer that does it is not subject to background-tab throttling because a wall display is by definition the FOREGROUND tab. The natural kiosk page also self-updates: alert-hub is one of three pages that refresh data on a timer, so the surface most likely to be mounted on a wall does not freeze at whatever it loaded with. ★THE GAP was recovery. This platform's error idiom is whListError with a manual Retry BUTTON - correct for a person holding a phone, useless on a screen nobody touches, where recovery must be automatic or it never happens. And the one moment a long-lived page KNOWS its data may be stale - regaining the network - was already being observed and thrown away: nav-hub listened for 'online' only to repaint its connectivity pill. ★FIX: the reconnect now also re-runs the community activity check, sharing the debounce added for the cross-tab path in T144. checkCommunityActivity already fails closed without a session, so a reconnect on a signed-out page costs nothing. This closes the specific hole T144 recorded as remaining ('converges a tab whose data went STALE, not one that missed NEW activity') for the blip case - a display that loses and regains its link now re-reads instead of showing an hours-old count. Verified: file parses, and the listener at indent 4 correctly closes over checkCommunityActivity (497) and _seenDebounce (568) at IIFE level, both initialised during setup long before any event can fire. ★STILL OPEN, deliberately: a page that never loses the network and never reloads still will not see new activity - only polling or realtime fixes that, and adding a timer to shared chrome on 31 pages to serve best-effort chrome is the wrong trade. A dedicated wall MODE (larger type, no chrome, aggressive refresh) is the scoped product decision this trajectory exists to surface, not something to infer. pct 65 -> 80. || LOCKING->90 2026-09-01: FINISHED (fix+gate) - all assigned gates (auto-read-retry) PASS standalone; property proven, board flips to locked. pct -> 90. ||2026-09-02 PROMOTED locking->locked by post_board_promote on the full board (1043 PASS / 24 FAIL, mode full; all named gates PASS). pct -> 100. · [2026-09-05] WALKED LIVE 2026-09-07 via tools/prove_device_reality.mjs (gate device-reality), measured AT the viewport rather than in a media query, because a CSS breakpoint proves an intention and only rendering at 740x360 proves the content survived it. trajectories.title: Duplicate names: two "Pump 1"s
trajectories.basis: the SEEDED DATA already carries the fixture (two 'Atlas Copco GA75+ VSD': AC-001 Compressor Room / AC-002 Pump Pit 1) and the flagship picker DISTINGUISHES them fully: tag-first label + location + criticality per option. Aggregation poison structurally answered: machine is keyed on the TAG platform-wide (the mirror fix's own contract), never the display name. Remaining: name-only displays sweep in reports/searches + voice-router disambiguation walk (wave close).  || THE AGGREGATION-POISON HAZARD MEASURED 2026-08-26, and it is REAL BUT NOT YET ACTIVE. SEVEN reliability functions group logbook rows by the machine NAME and none uses asset_node_id: get_mtbf_by_machine, get_mttr_by_machine, get_failure_frequency, get_downtime_pareto, get_repeat_failures, get_oee_by_machine, compute_anomaly_signals. Names are not unique - this database holds 24 DUPLICATE ASSET NAMES inside a single hive ('Caterpillar 3516B' twice, 'Cummins QSK60-G4' twice), which is not bad data entry but a plant that bought two identical generators. WHY TODAY'S NUMBERS ARE STILL CORRECT IS LUCK: measured, ZERO machine strings map to more than one asset_node_id and ZERO duplicated names appear in the logbook, because nobody has yet logged a repair against the SECOND Caterpillar. The moment somebody does, its failures merge into the first one's MTBF, its downtime joins that Pareto bar, and its anomalies are scored against a history that is not its own - silently, in numbers a supervisor uses to choose a maintenance strategy for a machine that may be about to fail. DELIBERATELY NOT RE-KEYED HERE: changing seven functions to group on asset_node_id reshapes every reliability surface in the analytics UI, and that is a design decision to be made, not slipped in at the end of a sweep - so it is written up for Ian with the measurement that makes it cheap (98% of logbook rows already carry asset_node_id). WHAT IS BUILT is the alarm: gate name-keyed-aggregates fails the moment a machine string maps to >1 asset or a duplicated name appears in the logbook. Teeth-proven by staging that exact future - a repair logged against the second duplicate-named asset turned it RED - then removing the probe rows and confirming zero remain. A clean run means the collision has not happened, never that it cannot. || DUPLICATE NAMES ARE REAL HERE AND THE PLATFORM HANDLES THEM (2026-08-27). The scenario is not hypothetical: within ONE hive, 17 assets share a name with another - three 'Atlas Copco GA75+ VSD', two 'Beumer BE 250', and more. Every one of the 17 carries a DISTINCT tag (AC-001 / AC-002 / AC-003, in the Compressor Room, Pump Pit 1 and Boiler Room), and that is not luck: asset_nodes_tag_unique_per_hive is a UNIQUE INDEX on (hive_id, tag), so the database refuses a second AC-001 in the same plant. The logbook picker leads with the TAG and follows with the name (COLS aliases asset_id:tag), so the three compressors render as three distinguishable rows rather than one repeated three times - and its search folds diacritics (T128) across tag, name AND location, so 'Pena' finds 'Peña Line 2' and a location narrows a shared model name. ★I NEARLY FILED THE OPPOSITE, BY FORGETTING THE TENANT. My first query counted 45 distinct tags across 75 duplicate-named rows and I had a defect half-written - two rows sharing tag BLR-003 in different locations, a picker that could not tell them apart. Then the unique index made it impossible, and the reason was in my own SQL: no hive_id filter. The collisions were ACROSS PLANTS, where every plant legitimately has its own BLR-001. On a multi-tenant platform, a cross-tenant comparison is not a finding, it is a missing WHERE clause - and this is the most apt place in the codebase to have made that mistake. Remaining: the name-ambiguity sweep over REPORTS that aggregate by name rather than id (the pm_assets/asset_nodes name-join noted in T133 is exactly that risk). || ★DUPLICATES ARE REAL, THE DATA LAYER IS SAFE, THE MATCH LAYER IS NOT (2026-08-28). First, this is not hypothetical: 24 asset names are duplicated WITHIN a single hive in local data (parts: 0). Two machines really do share a name here. ★THE AGGREGATION-POISON HAZARD THIS TRAJECTORY NAMES DOES NOT EXIST. Only one view groups by a name column - v_pm_compliance_truth - and reading its clause settles it: GROUP BY pa.hive_id, pa.id, pa.asset_name, pa.tag_id, ... The primary key is IN the grouping, so asset_name is carried as a LABEL, not used as the key; two same-named assets keep separate compliance rows. Correct SQL, and the concern was worth checking rather than assuming. ★WHERE AMBIGUITY SURVIVES is the logbook's inline PM panel, which does not pick an asset - it MATCHES one from a typed string, comparing lowercase asset_name AND tag_id with substring containment in BOTH directions (al.includes(ml) || ml.includes(al)). With duplicate names a typed 'Pump 1' matches several rows, assetIds collects them ALL, and the panel projects PM signals for the union - labelled with asset_name, which is the same string for every one of them. A 100% failure rate is never a finding. || THE AUDIT IS NOW A TOOL, AND BUILDING IT EXPOSED A THIRD INSTRUMENT BUG (2026-08-28). tools/check_locked_gates_are_green.py makes the question repeatable - it reads the registry and the board, runs every python gate behind a chosen status, and REPORTS. It also distinguishes TIMEOUT from FAIL, because conflating them is what made the hand-run audit's first answer wrong. ★AND ITS OWN FIRST READING WAS A FALSE FINDING: it reported T2's live-page-journeys as 'named by the registry, not on the board'. The gate is registered and runnable - it is simply written INLINE, `{"id": ..., "script": ...}` on one line, while my pattern required a newline between the two keys. Whitespace-flexible now, and the correction is larger than the one gate: the pattern was discovering 831 board entries when there are 976, so it had been blind to 145 of them - a reader that silently sees 85% of a file will eventually accuse something innocent. Every one of the six rows found this way was inflated, never deflated, which is the direction drift always takes when nothing checks it: the number a reader trusts drifts up while the narrative underneath it says otherwise. trajectories.title: Maximum-length everything
trajectories.basis: census + adoption on BOTH leader pages: marketplace post-desc (0/2000 proven at 390) and project-manager's four biggest caps (wiz-desc/f-desc 2000, s-notes 1000, co-scope 2000) now carry the community counter idiom; both pages load clean. community/asset-hub already adopted; voice-journal states its cap in the label. Filled every capped input to its longest LEGAL value - a single unbroken 'WWWW...' token, deliberately, because a wrapping-friendly sentence hides an overflow that a real part number would expose - and asserted the value neither widens the page nor pushes its own field past the right edge. RESULT: 10 visible capped fields across six pages, 0 breaking. ★BUT THE DENOMINATOR IS THE FINDING: 66 capped fields EXIST on those pages and only 10 are visible at rest. inventory, logbook, project-manager, community and pm-scheduler each reported ZERO - not because they have no caps, but because their forms live behind modals and panels that a resting sweep never opens. Recording '66 fields, 0 break' would have been a skipped partition reading as a covered one; what is actually proven is the 10 reachable ones. The other 56 need their flows DRIVEN, which is exactly what prove_flow_fits_the_floor.mjs already does for the floor viewport - folding an at-cap fill into that harness is the real remaining unit, not a second resting sweep. ★AND THE FIRST CUT PRODUCED 18 FALSE FINDINGS: the same three fields on every page (wh-fb-subject/body/email), which are the CLOSED feedback drawer - visibility:hidden, parked at x=754 against a 390 viewport. I had measured geometry without asking whether anyone can see it, so an off-screen closed panel read as six pages of broken layout. The probe now walks the ancestor chain for display/visibility/opacity before measuring anything. Remaining: the at-cap fill folded into the flow-driving harness (the 56 behind modals) + truncation-with-full-access. || THE 56 BEHIND MODALS ARE NOW REACHED, AND THE PARTITION IS CLOSED (2026-08-28). tools/prove_at_cap_fits.mjs drives seven flows OPEN - inventory's #part-modal, marketplace's post/inquiry/RFQ forms, community's composer, and logbook's wizard steps 2 and 3 including the extras drawer - then fills every capped field there to its longest legal value and asserts it neither widens the page nor pushes its own field past the right edge. 18 capped fields at 390, 0 breaking. (1) Measuring geometry without VISIBILITY produced 18 'defects' that were one CLOSED feedback drawer (visibility:hidden, parked at x=754 against a 390 viewport) counted once per page. (2) Guessing the surface selector - '#part-form, #add-part-modal, form' when the real container is #part-modal - reached 0 of inventory's 4 visible fields and reported ok, while the opener logged success: a prover that opens the RIGHT form and measures the WRONG box is indistinguishable from a clean run. So every flow now declares how many fields it EXPECTS, and under-reach FAILS rather than passing as a quiet zero - which immediately caught a third gap, logbook's extras drawer sitting inside an inactive wizard step. A flow that reached nothing (#use-modal, needs a stocked part selected first) was DELETED rather than kept as a decorative green. GATE at-cap-fits registered, teeth 7/7 - every flow with fields goes red when its container is widened, each verified clean=0 beforehand.
